unit.can_do_en: plan a walk in the forest and talk about berries.

brief.situation_en: Monday at work. Ville asks Maria about her weekend.

lines.speaker: Ville
lines.gloss_en: Where were you at the weekend?

judge.reason: sä/sinä is only a register difference; the question is the same.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: I was at a cottage by a lake.

judge.reason: mä/minä is only a register difference; place and facts are the same.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Ainon perheen. Me tultiin takas eilen.
lines.text_kirja: Ainon perheen. Me tulimme takaisin eilen.
lines.gloss_en: Aino's family's. We came back yesterday.

judge.reason: tultiin takas is the colloquial form of tulimme takaisin; both say 'we came back yesterday'.

lines.speaker: Ville
lines.gloss_en: Did you swim in the lake?

judge.reason: Uitteks/järves are colloquial forms of uitteko/järvessä; both ask 'did you swim in the lake?'.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Joo! Ja me mentiin soutuveneel saareen.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä! Ja me menimme soutuveneellä saareen.
lines.gloss_en: Yes! And we rowed to an island.

judge.reason: Joo/kyllä both mean yes; mentiin soutuveneel is the colloquial form of menimme soutuveneellä; the island and rowboat are unchanged.

lines.speaker: Ville
lines.gloss_en: That sounds like a proper Finnish summer.

judge.reason: ihan and aivan are synonyms meaning 'quite/totally'; the rest is identical.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: It was the best weekend ever!

judge.reason: ikinä and koskaan both mean 'ever' in this context; the meaning is the same.

forms.why_en: Inessive of 'mikä': here it means 'where', asking about a place.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
olla means to be. -i- marks the past and -t goes with sinä: olit.
Viikonloppu with -na for 'at, on' a time: viikonloppuna.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
Olla, to be, in the past tense with -n for 'I': olin.
Mökki with -llä for 'at', and kk turns to k: mökillä.
rannalla, 'on the shore', needs -n on the word before: järvi becomes järven.
Adds -lla for 'on': ranta becomes rannalla, nt turning into nn.
kuka, who, becomes kenen for 'whose'.
Adds -n for 'of': perhe becomes perheen, 'of the family'.
Me means we. Speech says it the same way.
Speech uses tultiin with me, 'we'. Books write tulimme, with -i- for the past.
Speech shortens takaisin to takas. Books write takaisin.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: past tense, 2nd person plural, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: uida, to swim. -i- marks the past and -tte goes with te: uitte. -ko asks. Speech uses -ks: uitteks.
Te is 'you' when you talk to more than one person. People say it the same way.
Adds -ssä for 'in': järvi becomes järvessä. Speech drops the last vowel: järves.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.
And: joins the coffee and the bun in the order.
Speech uses mentiin with me, 'we'. Books write menimme, with -i- for the past.
Adds -llä for 'by': soutuvene becomes soutuveneellä. Speech drops the last vowel: soutuveneel.
Adds -en for 'to': saari becomes saareen.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Ihan is the everyday spoken word. Books write aivan.
kuulostaa, to seem by the sound of it, takes -lta: suomalainen becomes suomalaiselta.
kuulostaa, to seem by the sound of it, takes -ltä: kesä becomes kesältä.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
Olla, to be, in the past tense for he, she or it: oli.
The superlative of hyvä, good: paras, best.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech often says ikinä. Books write koskaan. With en, both mean 'never'.
